$28 an Hour Is How Much a Year? $58,240 Full-Time, Before Taxes

Direct Answer$28 an hour is $58,240 a year full-time ($1,120 a week, $4,853.33 a month) before taxes. Schedules, overtime, a bonus, and exact federal take-home inside.

Gross pay estimates

Quick Answer

$28 an hour is $58,240 a year full-time before taxes — $1,120 a week and $4,853.33 a month.

The Short Answer: $58,240 a Year

At $28 an hour on a standard full-time schedule — 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year — you earn $58,240 a year before taxes. The formula is one multiplication: hourly rate × hours per week × weeks per year. Here that is $28 × 40 × 52 = $58,240, or 2,080 paid hours in the year. The rest of this guide is that number under real-life pressure: fewer hours, overtime hours, unpaid weeks, what federal taxes leave behind, what a $2,000 bonus is really worth after withholding, what one extra overtime hour a week adds, and whether $28 an hour counts as a good wage.

Two figures you may meet elsewhere need settling before you trust them. Some sites count 2,000 hours (50 paid weeks) and quote $56,000 — that assumes two unpaid weeks, and the unpaid-weeks section below prices that case exactly. Others count every weekday in the year (2,088 hours) and quote $58,464 — that counts public holidays as paid workdays, which most jobs do not. Neither is the standard full-time year. Employers, payroll systems, and this guide use 2,080 hours, and every variation in this guide is measured against it so the numbers stay comparable with our other wage guides.

$28 an Hour in Every Pay Period

One hourly rate, six ways to see it. All figures below are gross pay, before any tax or deduction:

PeriodHoursGross Pay
Hour1$28.00
Day (8 hours)8$224.00
Week (40 hours)40$1,120.00
Biweekly (80 hours)80$2,240.00
Semi-monthly (24 checks)—$2,426.67
Month (average)173.33$4,853.33
Year (2,080 hours)2,080$58,240.00

Figure 1: $28 an hour across pay periods. The semi-monthly check is larger only because there are fewer of them — the year is the same.

The monthly line is the one people misread most. $4,853.33 is an average: a four-week month pays $4,480, and a three-paycheck biweekly month pays $6,720 gross. If you budget from a three-paycheck month, you will overspend in the next one. Our biweekly vs semi-monthly guide explains the check-size difference.

$28 an Hour at Different Schedules

Not everyone works 40 hours. The same rate at different weekly hours gives very different years:

Hours per weekWeeklyMonthly (average)Annual
20 (part-time)$560.00$2,426.67$29,120.00
25 (part-time)$700.00$3,033.33$36,400.00
30 (part-time)$840.00$3,640.00$43,680.00
35$980.00$4,246.67$50,960.00
40 (full-time)$1,120.00$4,853.33$58,240.00

Two schedule details trip people up. First, a 37.5-hour paid week — common where a daily unpaid lunch is excluded from paid hours — pays $54,600 a year, which is $3,640 less than the full 40-hour figure even though the job still fills your whole week. Second, part-time roles often come without the benefits a full-time role carries, so compare total compensation, not just the hourly number. Our full-time hours guide explains where the 40-hour line comes from, and the bonus and weekly-overtime sections below price the two most common extras — a year-end bonus and a single weekly overtime hour — in full.

What Overtime Adds

Overtime is where an hourly rate pulls away from a salary. At time-and-a-half, each overtime hour pays $42 instead of $28. With 5 overtime hours every week, all year:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Regular pay40 hours × $28$1,120.00 per week
Step 2 — Overtime rate$28 × 1.5$42.00 per hour
Step 3 — Overtime pay5 hours × $42$210.00 per week
Step 4 — Weekly total$1,120 + $210$1,330.00 per week
Annual total$1,330 × 52$69,160.00

Five steady overtime hours add $10,920 a year — nearly a fifth of the base salary, and the reason an hourly offer with reliable overtime can beat a higher-looking salary that pays nothing past 40 hours. Our overtime calculation guide works through the same math with the overtime calculator.

What Unpaid Weeks Cost

Paid weeks are part of the offer, not a footnote. At $28 an hour, each unpaid week costs exactly $1,120 of gross pay:

Paid weeksPaid hoursAnnual gross
52 (fully paid year)2,080$58,240.00
50 (2 unpaid weeks)2,000$56,000.00
48 (4 unpaid weeks)1,920$53,760.00

Notice the middle row: two unpaid weeks land you on exactly $56,000 — the same figure some sites quote as the full-time answer. It is not the full-time answer; it is the two-unpaid-weeks answer. Ask how many weeks are paid before accepting any hourly offer, because two unpaid weeks quietly erase $2,240 from the headline number.

$28 an Hour After Taxes (Federal Only)

Gross pay is not spending money. For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, here is the federal-only sketch — state tax, 401(k), and health premiums are excluded, so your real paycheck will be lower:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay$28 × 2,080 hours$58,240.00
Step 2 — Standard deductionSingle filer, 2026− $16,100.00
Step 3 — Taxable income$58,240 − $16,100$42,140.00
Step 4 — Federal income tax10% × $12,400 + 12% × $29,740$4,808.80
Step 5 — FICA$58,240 × 7.65% (SS $3,610.88 + Medicare $844.48)$4,455.36
Take-home (federal only)$58,240 − $4,808.80 − $4,455.36$48,975.84

That is $4,081.32 a month on average, or $1,883.69 per biweekly paycheck, before state tax — about $23.55 of take-home for every hour worked. Two rates are worth separating: your marginal bracket is 12% (the rate on your last dollars), but your effective federal rate is only 8.3% ($4,808.80 ÷ $58,240), because the first $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10%. You keep 84.1% of gross after federal taxes alone. One warning about the search results: at least two ranking pages contradict themselves on this very rate — one quotes roughly $45,427 in its summary but $48,975.84 in its own detail, and another headlines $48,976 while its listed federal, Social Security, and Medicare figures add up to $48,834.34. Trust the bracket steps above, not a page that disagrees with itself. The FICA piece uses the same 7.65% explained in our FICA guide, and the same annual-liability method drives our paycheck tax guide — which is why some online calculators show a slightly different number: they annualize a single paycheck's withholding instead of computing the year's liability. Our pay stub guide shows where each of these lines lands on a real stub.

Honesty note: this sketch assumes all $58,240 counts as wages for both income tax and FICA, with no pre-tax deductions. A 401(k) contribution would lower the income-tax lines but not the FICA lines; cafeteria-plan health premiums would lower both.

What a $2,000 Bonus Is Really Worth

A bonus is the one paycheck that regularly disappoints people, because it is withheld differently from regular pay. Employers usually withhold federal income tax on a bonus at the flat 22% supplemental rate, not at your 12% marginal bracket — and FICA still applies on top. Here is a $2,000 year-end bonus priced honestly:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — BonusStated bonus$2,000.00
Step 2 — Federal supplemental withholding$2,000 × 22%− $440.00
Step 3 — FICA$2,000 × 7.65%− $153.00
Bonus in hand (before state tax)$2,000 − $440 − $153$1,407.00

Two things soften that haircut. First, the 22% is withholding, not your final tax: when you file, the bonus is taxed with the rest of your income at your real brackets, so part of the $440 typically comes back as a refund if your overall rate is lower — the $1,407 is cash in hand now, not the bonus's final after-tax value. Second, compare it with the alternative: a $2,000 bonus is worth more than a $1-an-hour raise held for only part of the year, but less than a permanent $1 raise, which pays $2,080 gross every full year. Judge a bonus offer on whether it repeats, not on the headline number.

What One Extra Overtime Hour a Week Adds

Five overtime hours every week is a big commitment. One extra hour a week is the version most people can actually sustain — staying an hour late, or covering one short shift extension — and it is worth pricing on its own, because it compounds quietly:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — One overtime hour, gross52 weeks × $42.00$2,184.00 a year
Step 2 — Take-home on that hour$2,184 × (1 − 12% − 7.65%)$1,754.84 a year
New annual totals$58,240 + $2,184 gross$60,424 gross, $50,730.68 take-home

One hour a week lifts the year past $60,000 gross and adds $1,754.84 of take-home, for 52 extra hours — about $33.75 of take-home per extra hour. The take-home step is honest, too: the extra dollars are taxed at your 12% marginal rate plus 7.65% FICA, so you keep 80.35% of them, and the 22% bracket still does not touch you (taxable income at $60,424 is $44,324, still below $50,400). The caveat is the same as ever: the hour only pays time-and-a-half if it pushes you past 40 hours in that week and you are non-exempt — an extra hour inside a 40-hour week is paid at the regular $28 rate, worth $1,456 gross for the year instead of $2,184.

Is $28 an Hour a Good Wage?

By the national yardstick, yes. Recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data puts the national median hourly wage at $22.26, so $28 an hour sits $5.74 above the typical American worker — $11,939.20 a year above the median full-time year — and about 3.9 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage. It also clears the $55,000 line by $3,240 and lands within $1,760 of a $60,000 salary, which is where many job postings start describing a role as a mid-level position rather than an entry-level one.

Whether it feels good depends on the same two things as every other rate: rent and benefits. In a low-cost city, $4,081.32 of monthly federal-only take-home covers a modest life with room to save; in a high-rent city, the same paycheck can feel tight once state tax and health premiums come out. Judge the offer on the whole package — paid weeks, health premiums, retirement match, schedule control, and any overtime on offer — not on the hourly number alone.

Limitations

  1. Federal only: the after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. State and local income taxes are excluded, so actual take-home is lower; the after-tax sketch is federal only.
  2. Benefits excluded: 401(k) contributions, health premiums, and other deductions come out of your check and are not counted here, except in the bonus section where the withholding-vs-liability difference is noted.
  3. Overtime is conditional: the $69,160 overtime figure and the $60,424 weekly-overtime figure need non-exempt status, actual overtime hours, and an employer that pays past 40 hours.
  4. Schedule assumption: figures use the schedule stated in each section; fewer hours or unpaid weeks change every number.
  5. Withholding vs liability: a single paycheck's withholding can differ from this annual-liability sketch; the difference settles when you file your return.
  6. Not tax advice: the take-home sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction. Credits, other income, and filing status change your real return.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about $28 an hour:

How much is $28 an hour a year?

Full-time, $58,240 a year before taxes: $28 × 40 hours a week × 52 weeks. That is $4,853.33 a month on average, $2,240 per biweekly paycheck, and $1,120 a week. Part-time hours, overtime, or unpaid weeks change the total — the schedules section above works through each case.

How much is $28 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer in 2026, the federal-only sketch is $48,975.84 a year: $58,240 gross minus $4,808.80 federal income tax and $4,455.36 FICA. State income tax, 401(k) contributions, and health premiums would reduce the paycheck further — they are not in this sketch. Note the marginal bracket is still 12%, not 22%: taxable income of $42,140 sits $8,260 below the $50,400 threshold where the 22% bracket starts.

How much is $28 an hour biweekly?

Gross, $2,240 per biweekly paycheck (80 hours). After federal tax alone, the biweekly take-home averages $1,883.69. Do not confuse biweekly with semi-monthly: a semi-monthly check is $2,426.67 gross, larger only because there are 24 checks a year instead of 26 — the annual total is the same $58,240.

How much is $28 an hour a month?

On average, $4,853.33 a month gross — the annual $58,240 divided by 12. After federal tax alone, the monthly take-home averages $4,081.32. But no single month is average: a four-week month pays $4,480 gross, and a three-paycheck biweekly month pays $6,720 gross. Budget from the average, not from any one month.

Is $28 an hour a good wage?

Yes, by the national yardstick: recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data puts the national median hourly wage at $22.26, so $28 an hour sits $5.74 above the typical American worker — $11,939.20 a year above the median full-time year — and about 3.9 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage. Whether it feels good depends mostly on your rent, your state tax, and the benefits wrapped around it.

What is time and a half for $28 an hour?

Time and a half is $42 an hour ($28 × 1.5). With 5 overtime hours every week, all year, the annual gross rises from $58,240 to $69,160 — an extra $10,920. The overtime section above works through the weekly steps, and the weekly-overtime section shows what a single extra overtime hour a week is worth instead.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $28 an hour is $58,240 a year full-time ($1,120 a week, $2,240 biweekly, $4,853.33 a month on average), before taxes.
  • Budget from the average month, not any single month — four-week months pay $4,480, three-paycheck months pay $6,720.
  • Five overtime hours a week add $10,920 a year ($69,160 total) — if you are non-exempt and actually work them.
  • Each unpaid week costs $1,120: ask how many weeks are paid before accepting any hourly offer.
  • A $2,000 bonus puts $1,407 in hand before state tax — the 22% supplemental withholding partly comes back when you file.
  • One extra overtime hour a week adds $1,754.84 of take-home and lifts the year past $60,000 gross — only if it pushes you past 40 hours.
  • You are still in the 12% bracket: $42,140 of taxable income sits $8,260 below the 22% threshold — ignore pages that claim otherwise.
  • Federal-only take-home is $48,975.84 for a single filer — 12% marginal bracket, but only an 8.3% effective federal rate.
  • Compare on annual gross first, then take-home, then benefits — $28 an hour beats a $55,000 salary by $3,240 gross.

Sources & Method

Gross figures use the standard full-time year of 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks); monthly averages divide the annual total by 12 and biweekly figures use 26 paychecks. The after-tax sketch uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: standard deduction $16,100, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 of taxable income, per IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), with the full $58,240 below the wage base. The median-wage comparison uses recent Bureau of Labor Statistics data (median hourly wage $22.26). State income tax, retirement contributions, health premiums, bonuses, and tips are excluded except where a note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Full-time gross pay is $58,240 a year — $1,120 a week, $4,853.33 a month.
  2. Part-time, overtime, unpaid weeks, the bonus case, and the one-overtime-hour-a-week case change the picture — the guide works through each case.
  3. Whether $28 an hour covers a comfortable life depends on your rent and location — it sits above the national median, not below it.
